analysis.one_liner: Orders FDA to recall all e-cigarettes that haven't passed safety review.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in November 2019 and never advanced further before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Food and Drug Administration, within 60 days, to order every e-cigarette and vape product that has not cleared the agency's premarket safety review off the market — a mandatory recall covering manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers. It would also write into law that these devices count as tobacco products under federal food and drug law and that they cannot claim an exemption from premarket review. The bill was introduced by Representative Mark DeSaulnier, a Democrat from California, but it drew no cosponsors and never got a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Teenagers and young people who would otherwise buy flavored and unreviewed vape products, and adults who want assurance that the nicotine devices sold on every corner have actually been reviewed for safety. Parents and schools dealing with youth vaping also gain from products being pulled pending review.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA, within 60 days of enactment, to issue an order requiring manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers to immediately stop distributing and recall every e-cigarette product that has not received a premarket review order [S3].

Amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to state explicitly that electronic nicotine delivery systems — e-cigarettes, vape pens, e-hookah, e-cigars, and related devices and their parts and liquids — are tobacco products subject to FDA authority [S3].

Closes the loophole the bill targets by deeming e-cigarettes not substantially equivalent to older tobacco products, so the premarket review requirement applies to them starting 60 days after enactment [S3].
The recall order must include notice to people exposed to the risks from these products, an informal hearing within 10 days, a recall timetable, and periodic progress reports to the FDA [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Vape manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers, who would have to pull unreviewed products from the market within weeks. Adult vapers who rely on these products, including people using them to quit cigarettes, would lose access to devices until and unless they cleared review. The FDA would take on the cost of running the recall.
analysis.who_pays_short: Vape makers, shops, and adult users

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates a near-total market removal with no safety-based screen: every ENDS product is ordered recalled simply because it has not completed review, even if review might later clear it, and an order can be withdrawn only once a premarket review order is issued for that product [S3].

Adult smokers who use e-cigarettes to stay off cigarettes would lose access to devices during the recall, a real cost for the population the FDA has generally viewed as less harmed by vaping than by smoking [S3].
A rapid recall across thousands of retail locations would be difficult to enforce, and the bill allows FDA to enlist retailers' help with notice only where those persons can be identified [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health logic is straightforward: in 2019 youth vaping was rising fast and unreviewed products were on the market, and this bill would force every one of them through safety review or off the shelf. The cost falls on a legal industry and on adult users, some of whom use these products as a less harmful alternative to cigarettes. The blunt, no-exemptions recall design trades that adult-access cost for speed and certainty, which supporters would call justified and critics would call overbroad.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mark DeSaulnier (D-CA) introduced the bill on November 8, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
Four days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no markup, vote, or further action is recorded for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: E-cigarette manufacturers and vape retailers, whose products stayed on the market instead of being recalled pending review.

for.name: Rep. Mark DeSaulnier
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter on the record; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Frank Pallone, D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opponents acted on the record, so the partisan split cannot be measured; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would order every product they sell recalled and removed from distribution unless and until it passes FDA premarket review, wiping out sales of unreviewed devices within 60 days [S3]. Keeping the products on the market without review is worth billions in sales; the industry's interest in blocking the bill runs against the push to keep unreviewed nicotine devices away from teenagers [S3].
Retailers would be ordered to immediately cease distribution and pull products from shelves, losing revenue on inventory that would be recalled [S3].

industries.industry: Adult vaping consumers (people using e-cigarettes to quit smoking)
industries.note: Adult users would lose access to devices during the recall period, though a cleared, reviewed market could eventually return safer products [S3].
